newsitem.title: USA: Rollins, Laidlaw expect agreement in two weeks.
newsitem.headline: Rollins, Laidlaw expect agreement in two weeks.

text.p: Rollins Environmental Services Inc and Laidlaw Inc expect to sign a definitive agreement in two weeks for the merger of Laidlaw's hazardous waste management operations into Rollins, company chairman John Rollins told Reuters Friday.

In an interview after what was probably the company's last annual meeting in its present form, chairman Rollins said "It's something we've been striving to do: to get a company that's balanced. Laidlaw ties in with our company because they pick up waste and we incinerate it."
Rollins said he expects the merger to be completed by May assuming it is approved by government regulatory commissions and Rollins shareholders.
Rollins Environmental will be renamed Laidlaw Environmental Services Inc and its stock will trade on the New York Stock Exchange.

Laidlaw shareholders will receive a package worth about $900 million including $400 million cash, $350 million of 12 year five percent convertible debentures and a new issue of 120 million shares of Rollins common stock.
The 60 million shares of Rollins common stock now trading at 2-3/4 a share would bring the combined number of oustanding shares in the new company to 180 million.
Laidlaw would own 66 percent of the new company and the remaining 34 percent would continue to be publicly traded. Analysts have estimated combined annual revenues would be in excess of $1 billion.

A 10 member board would consist of three Laidlaw nominees, three Rollins nominees, three outside directors, and Laidlaw president Kenneth Winger, who would become chief executive of the merged company.

Following the Jan 6 announcement of the proposed merger, the California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS) withdrew a proxy proposal calling for more independent Rollins directors. The company has been criticized by shareholders for falling revenues in recent years.
It is estimated that consolidation following the merger would eliminate at least 900 jobs and reduce annual costs by $75 million.
